{
 "id": "Q61",
 "sourceFile": "Thoracolumbar fascia and lumbar muscle stiffness in athletes with a history of hamstring injury.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The title 'Thoracolumbar Fascia and Lumbar Muscle Stiffness in Athletes with A History of Hamstring Injury' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Case-control Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Adult / Recreational", "Healthy Athletes", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A comparison of 13 healthy amateur soccer players with no hamstring injury history and 11 players with a grade II biceps femoris long head strain in the past year (about 7.4 months earlier). Shear-wave elastography of the thoracolumbar fascia, erector spinae and multifidus was measured at knee angles of 0, 45 and 90 degrees and during prone trunk extension. The authors report higher fascia and paraspinal modulus in the injured group (passive fascia group effect F(1,22) = 15.79, P = 0.0001), higher passive EMG and lower knee flexion torque in the injured group.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The design is retrospective, so the authors cannot say whether the differences were present before injury, and the groups are small (13 and 11). Rehabilitation was not recorded, elastography depends on probe position, and temperature was not controlled.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the higher fascia stiffness as a cause of hamstring re-injury and treat lumbar fascia as a proven target, but the design is retrospective and the authors note that stiffness may already have been present before the injury.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2024,
   "citation": "Kellis E, Kekelekis A, Drakonaki EE. Thoracolumbar Fascia and Lumbar Muscle Stiffness in Athletes with a History of Hamstring Injury. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2024;23:436-444.",
   "doi": "10.52082/jssm.2024.436",
   "abstract": "Compared shear-wave elastography stiffness of the thoracolumbar fascia, erector spinae and multifidus in 13 soccer players without and 11 with a previous hamstring injury, during passive and active knee flexion and trunk extension.",
   "tldr": "Soccer players with a hamstring strain about seven months earlier had stiffer lumbar fascia and paraspinal muscles than uninjured players in this small study. Consider assessing lumbopelvic tissue in players with a hamstring history, but the study does not show that this stiffness causes re-injury.",
   "methods": "Comparison of 13 healthy amateur male soccer players with 11 male players who had a grade II biceps femoris long head strain in the past year. Shear-wave elastography measured tissue modulus at three knee flexion angles and during trunk extension, alongside surface EMG and maximal isometric knee flexion torque.",
   "findings": "Fascia modulus was higher in the injured group in passive testing (group effect P = 0.0001) and in active testing (P < 0.05), and erector spinae and multifidus modulus was also higher. Passive EMG was greater in the injured group, while knee flexion maximal torque was greater in the uninjured group. Spinal problems were present in some players in both groups, with no difference between groups.",
   "limitations": "The study is retrospective with no pre-injury measures, so pre-existing differences cannot be excluded. The samples are small, the rehabilitation protocol was not recorded, and SWE values depend on the probe position relative to the fibres. Temperature was not recorded.",
   "practicalImplications": "Staff could include lumbar fascia and paraspinal stiffness, and knee flexion strength, when assessing players with a previous hamstring strain. The authors suggest only that future studies test whether exercises for these tissues reduce re-injury.",
   "athleteDev": "The study does not measure performance. It does show that players with a previous hamstring strain produced lower knee flexion torque, which may matter when planning strength work for those players.",
   "rtp": "The study cannot be used as a return to play test or clearance criterion. Players were studied about seven months after a grade II strain, so it does not show whether these tissue differences exist or change during return to play."
 }
}

 "id": "Q63",
 "sourceFile": "Throwing cold water on muscle growth - A systematic review with meta-analysis of the effects of postexercise cold water immersion on resistance training-induced hypertrophy.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The title 'Throwing cold water on muscle growth: A systematic review with meta-analysis of the effects of postexercise cold water immersion on resistance training-induced hypertrophy' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A PRISMA-guided systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis of 8 randomized studies (young adults aged 20 to 26, mostly men, 4 to 12 weeks) comparing resistance training with and without cold water immersion applied after training. The comparative effect favoured resistance training alone (cSMD -0.22, 95% credible interval -0.47 to 0.04), which the authors describe as some evidence of attenuated hypertrophy. Study quality was fair to poor (mean SMART-LD score 9.8 of 20, with no study rated good).",
 "screeningLimitations": "The credible interval for the main comparison crosses zero, the pooled studies are small and short, and quality was rated fair to poor. Measurement methods varied widely, nutrition was rarely controlled, and the samples were mostly young men with cold water immersion given within 15 minutes after each session.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the attenuated-hypertrophy finding as a firm rule against post-training cold water immersion, but the credible interval includes zero and the evidence base is small and of fair to poor quality.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2024,
   "citation": "Piñero A, Burke R, Augustin F, Mohan AE, DeJesus K, Sapuppo M, et al. Throwing cold water on muscle growth: A systematic review with meta-analysis of the effects of postexercise cold water immersion on resistance training-induced hypertrophy. European Journal of Sport Science. 2024;1-13.",
   "doi": "10.1002/ejsc.12074",
   "abstract": "Systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis of 8 randomized studies comparing resistance training with and without postexercise cold water immersion on measures of muscle growth.",
   "tldr": "Cold water immersion straight after resistance training was associated with somewhat smaller muscle gains than resistance training alone, but the estimate is imprecise and the studies are of fair to poor quality. Staff whose priority is muscle size may want to consider timing, since the studies tested immersion within 15 minutes of training.",
   "methods": "PRISMA-guided search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science, with a three-level Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis. The eight included randomized studies applied cold water immersion within about 15 minutes after resistance sessions, and quality was rated with the SMART-LD tool and the Downs and Black checklist.",
   "findings": "Comparing resistance training with cold water immersion plus resistance training, the pooled effect favoured resistance training alone (cSMD -0.22, 95% CrI -0.47 to 0.04). Within-study effects were 0.36 (95% CrI 0.10 to 0.61) for resistance training and 0.14 (95% CrI -0.08 to 0.36) for cold water immersion plus resistance training. Meta-regression found no clear effect of training status, and no study was rated good quality.",
   "limitations": "Measurement methods varied (DXA, ultrasound, MRI, biopsy, circumference) and most studies did not control nutrition. Samples were mostly young men, loads were moderate, and only one study had a female sample. Results apply to immersion within about 15 minutes of training, not to other cooling methods or timings.",
   "practicalImplications": "If hypertrophy is the goal for a training block, staff could avoid immediate post-session cold water immersion or move it away from strength sessions, since this is the timing the studies tested. The evidence is weak and the effect may be small, so the decision should weigh recovery needs against the likely size of the muscle-growth cost.",
   "athleteDev": "For performance staff, the pooled data suggest that cold water immersion right after resistance sessions may slightly reduce muscle size gains compared with training alone. That matters most when hypertrophy is a training goal, and the review does not address strength or power outcomes.",
   "rtp": "The review excluded participants with musculoskeletal injury and studies healthy adults' muscle growth, so it cannot inform return to sport decisions."
 }
}

 "sports": ["American Football"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A retrospective analysis of NFL injury reports for every team and week of the 2012-13 to 2016-17 regular seasons (1,280 games, including 69 Thursday night games). The all-cause injury rate was 6,072 per 1,000 athletic exposures on Thursday nights versus 7,598 for weekend games, a relative risk of 0.97 (95% CI 0.95 to 0.98). The authors conclude that the shorter Thursday turnaround did not increase injury rates, and that eliminating Thursday games would be unlikely to lower them.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Injury reports give no injury type, severity or time lost, and the authors assumed every reported injury happened in a game. The analysis is short term, with 69 Thursday games, and the reported relative risk is described in the discussion as an absolute risk reduction of 3%, which is a mislabel.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the lower Thursday rate as proof that short recovery between games is safe, but the study measured only counts of reported injuries, not severity, time lost or longer-term outcomes.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2019,
   "citation": "Baker HP, Lee KY-H, Dayton SR, Terry M, Tjong VK. Thursday Night Football's impact on all-cause injuries in NFL players during 2012-2017. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2019.",
   "doi": "10.1080/00913847.2019.1587565",
   "abstract": "Compared all-cause injury rates in NFL players between Thursday night games and Sunday or Monday night games across five regular seasons, using weekly injury reports and injured reserve data.",
   "tldr": "Injury rates in Thursday night NFL games were slightly lower than in weekend games over five seasons, despite about three days of rest instead of six. Schedule changes that remove Thursday games are unlikely to reduce all-cause injuries on this evidence.",
   "methods": "Retrospective analysis of weekly NFL injury reports and injured reserve data for all 32 teams in the 2012-13 to 2016-17 regular seasons.
